topic: a prize-winning novel about a ferry captain
passage: Readers in the coastal town of Halden have long admired the local author Marta Velez. Her novel The Salt Orchard, a story about a ferry captain and her ______ won the regional fiction prize in 2021 and is now taught in several schools.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The appositive 'a story about a ferry captain and her grandson' opens with a comma after the title, so it must close with a comma before the verb 'won'.
steps: Find the main sentence: 'Her novel The Salt Orchard ... won the regional fiction prize.'
The words 'a story about a ferry captain and her grandson' are extra information about the novel.
The extra information opens with a comma after the title.
So it must close with a comma too: 'grandson,'.
strategy_tip: When a comma opens extra information, look for the end of that information and close it with a comma.

rationales.A: Correct. The comma closes the appositive that the comma after 'The Salt Orchard' opened, so the subject 'Her novel' connects cleanly to the verb 'won'.
rationales.B: Unclosed supplement: The appositive opens with a comma after the title, so it must also close with a comma before 'won'.
rationales.C: Semicolon before a fragment: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side, but 'Her novel The Salt Orchard, a story about a ferry captain and her grandson' has no verb.
rationales.D: Mixed marks: The appositive opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash. Use the same mark on both sides.

passage: The mountain village of Torvik has an unusual rule for new houses. Every roof must be painted dark ______ the dark color absorbs sunlight and helps melt the heavy snow that collects on the roofs each winter.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Both sides of the blank are complete sentences, and the second one explains the rule in the first. A colon can join them.
steps: Before the blank: 'Every roof must be painted dark gray.' Complete sentence.
After the blank: 'the dark color absorbs sunlight and helps melt the heavy snow...' Complete sentence.
The second sentence explains why the rule exists.
A colon joins two complete sentences when the second explains the first.
strategy_tip: If the second complete sentence explains the first, a colon is a safe choice; a comma alone is never enough.

rationales.A: Comma splice: A comma alone can't join two complete sentences.
rationales.B: Correct. The colon joins two complete sentences, and the second explains why the roofs must be dark gray.
rationales.C: Run-on sentence: Two complete sentences run together with no punctuation between them.
rationales.D: Semicolon before a fragment: 'because the dark color absorbs sunlight...' can't stand alone, so a semicolon can't come before it.

topic: a fern that grows in old wells
passage: Botanist Ilka Moreau studies a rare fern that grows only on the inner walls of old stone wells in the valley of Serrand. The fern needs constant shade and ______ it dries out within weeks if a well is left uncovered.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Both parts are complete sentences. A semicolon can join two complete sentences.
steps: Before the blank: 'The fern needs constant shade and moisture.' Complete sentence.
After the blank: 'it dries out within weeks if a well is left uncovered.' Complete sentence.
Two complete sentences need a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus 'and/but/so'.
Only the semicolon is offered, so choose 'moisture;'.
strategy_tip: Put your finger on the blank and test each side: two complete sentences need a semicolon or a period, not a comma.

rationales.A: Comma splice: A comma alone can't join two complete sentences.
rationales.B: Run-on sentence: Two complete sentences run together with no punctuation between them.
rationales.C: Correct. The semicolon joins two complete sentences about the fern.
rationales.D: Broken relative clause: 'which' needs to replace a noun in its clause, but 'which it dries out...' already has the subject 'it', so the clause doesn't work.

topic: a hiking badge for a mountain trail
passage: The Kessling Trail crosses three high mountain passes and takes most walkers about six weeks. Hikers who complete the full route in a single ______ a small bronze badge from the Kessling Walking Club.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is 'Hikers who complete the full route in a single summer' and the verb is 'receive'. No punctuation goes between a subject and its verb.
steps: Find the verb: 'receive'.
Ask who receives: 'Hikers who complete the full route in a single summer'. That whole phrase is the subject.
A subject and its verb are never separated by a single comma, semicolon, or dash.
Choose the option with no punctuation.
strategy_tip: A long subject still needs no punctuation before its verb; find the verb and check that nothing cuts it off.

rationales.A: Splits subject and verb: A single comma can't come between the subject 'Hikers who complete...' and the verb 'receive'.
rationales.B: Semicolon before a fragment: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side, and neither side is one here.
rationales.C: Splits subject and verb: A single dash can't come between the subject and the verb 'receive'.
rationales.D: Correct. No punctuation is needed between the long subject and its verb 'receive'.

topic: a timber beam in a sports hall roof
passage: Architect Petra Lindqvist designed the roof of the Hallam Sports Hall to carry heavy snow. Its central beam—the long curved part that carries the greatest share of the snow's ______ was made from layered timber rather than steel, because timber bends slightly under pressure instead of cracking.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The extra information 'the long curved part that carries the greatest share of the snow's weight' opens with a dash, so it must close with a dash before 'was made'.
steps: Find the main sentence: 'Its central beam ... was made from layered timber.'
The words between 'beam' and 'was' are extra information about the beam.
Look back: the extra information opens with a dash after 'beam'.
Close it with the same mark: 'weight—'.
strategy_tip: Before you choose, look back for the mark that opened the extra information; the closing mark must match it.

rationales.A: Correct. The dash closes the extra information that the dash after 'beam' opened, so 'Its central beam' connects to 'was made'.
rationales.B: Mixed marks: The extra information opens with a dash, so it can't close with a comma.
rationales.C: Unclosed supplement: Without a closing dash, the sentence reads as if 'the snow's weight was made from layered timber'.
rationales.D: Semicolon before a fragment: 'Its central beam—the long curved part...' has no verb, so it can't come before a semicolon.

topic: a film about a family of lamp-makers
passage: Director Anouk Delsaux had never made a feature film before she turned fifty. Her film Lanterns at Low Tide, a drama about a family of lamp-makers in the river town of ______ took six years to complete and won the jury prize at the Corvel Film Festival.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The appositive after the film's title opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma before the verb 'took'.
steps: Find the main sentence: 'Her film Lanterns at Low Tide ... took six years to complete.'
'a drama about a family of lamp-makers in the river town of Vellmar' describes the film; it is extra information.
It opens with a comma after the title, even though the blank comes many words later.
Close it with a comma: 'Vellmar,'.
strategy_tip: A long appositive after a title still needs a closing comma; find where the description ends and the verb begins.

rationales.A: Unclosed supplement: The appositive opens with a comma after the title, so it must close with a comma before 'took'.
rationales.B: Correct. The comma closes the appositive, so the subject 'Her film' connects to the verb 'took'.
rationales.C: Mixed marks: The appositive opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash.
rationales.D: Semicolon before a fragment: 'Her film Lanterns at Low Tide, a drama about...' has no verb, so it can't stand before a semicolon.

topic: an old sea turtle tagged decades ago
passage: Marine biologist Dara Okonjo tracks a group of sea turtles near the island of Pell. The oldest turtle in the group, a female that researchers first tagged in 1987 when she was already an ______ to the same beach every three years to lay her eggs.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The phrase 'a female that researchers first tagged in 1987 when she was already an adult' opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma before the verb 'returns'.
steps: Find the main sentence: 'The oldest turtle in the group ... returns to the same beach.'
The words from 'a female' to 'adult' describe the turtle; they are extra information.
The extra information opens with a comma after 'group'.
Close it with a comma before the verb: 'adult, returns'.
strategy_tip: Cross out the extra information; if the sentence still works, you found it, and its two marks must match.

rationales.A: Mixed marks: The extra information opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash.
rationales.B: Semicolon before a fragment: 'The oldest turtle in the group, a female that...' has no main verb, so it can't stand before a semicolon.
rationales.C: Correct. The comma closes the extra information that the comma after 'group' opened, so 'The oldest turtle' connects to 'returns'.
rationales.D: Unclosed supplement: Without a closing comma, the sentence reads as if 'she was already an adult returns to the same beach'.

topic: a debut novel about a young clockmaker
passage: Few first novels receive much attention from the critic Jonah Prell. Yet in his yearly review, Prell called Glass Harbor, Ines Barlow's novel about a young clockmaker who leaves her village to study in the ______ the most ambitious debut of the decade.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The appositive 'Ines Barlow's novel about a young clockmaker who leaves her village to study in the capital' opens with a comma after the title, so it must close with a comma.
steps: Find the main sentence: 'Prell called Glass Harbor the most ambitious debut of the decade.'
The words from 'Ines Barlow's novel' to 'capital' describe the book; they are extra information.
The extra information opens with a comma after the title 'Glass Harbor'.
Close it with a comma: 'capital,'.
strategy_tip: A 'who' clause inside an appositive doesn't end the appositive; close the whole description with the mark that opened it.

rationales.A: Unclosed supplement: The appositive opens with a comma after 'Glass Harbor', so it must also close with a comma.
rationales.B: Semicolon before a fragment: 'the most ambitious debut of the decade' has no verb, so it can't stand after a semicolon.
rationales.C: Mixed marks: The appositive opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash.
rationales.D: Correct. The comma closes the appositive about the book, and the sentence continues 'Prell called Glass Harbor ... the most ambitious debut'.

topic: sailors' letters found in an archive wall
passage: The Selmer Archive was founded in 1880 to collect records from the port of Selmer. The archive's oldest ______ a bundle of letters written by sailors in the 1790s—was found hidden inside a wall during repairs to the building in 2015.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The extra information 'a bundle of letters written by sailors in the 1790s' closes with a dash, so it must open with a dash after 'holding'.
steps: Find the main sentence: 'The archive's oldest holding ... was found hidden inside a wall.'
'a bundle of letters written by sailors in the 1790s' describes the holding; it is extra information.
Look ahead: the extra information closes with a dash after '1790s'.
Open it with the same mark: 'holding—'.
strategy_tip: The matching mark can come after the blank; read to the end of the sentence before you choose.

rationales.A: Correct. The dash opens the extra information, and the dash after '1790s' closes it.
rationales.B: Mixed marks: The extra information closes with a dash, so it can't open with a comma.
rationales.C: Colon after a fragment: A colon needs a complete sentence before it, but 'The archive's oldest holding' has no verb.
rationales.D: Unopened supplement: Without an opening dash, the closing dash after '1790s' has no partner, and 'holding a bundle of letters' reads as one phrase.

topic: benches facing away from a fountain
passage: While preparing a plan to redesign public spaces, urban planner Sela Marquand noticed something odd about the busiest square in the city of ______ every bench had been placed so that it faced away from the large fountain in the middle.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The first sentence says Marquand noticed 'something odd', and the second sentence names it. A colon introduces an explanation of the first complete sentence.
steps: Before the blank: 'While preparing a plan..., urban planner Sela Marquand noticed something odd about the busiest square in the city of Redfall.' Complete sentence (the 'While' phrase is only an opening).
After the blank: 'every bench had been placed so that it faced away from the large fountain...' Complete sentence.
The second sentence tells us what the 'something odd' was.
A colon joins them: 'Redfall:'.
strategy_tip: Words like 'something', 'one change', or 'a problem' in the first clause often point to a colon before the explanation.

rationales.A: Comma splice: The comma after the 'While' phrase doesn't change the rule; a comma alone still can't join two complete sentences.
rationales.B: Correct. The colon joins two complete sentences, and the second explains the 'something odd' that the first mentions.
rationales.C: Run-on sentence: Two complete sentences run together with no punctuation between them.
rationales.D: Broken relative clause: 'which' must stand for a noun inside its own clause, but the words after it already form a complete sentence, so the result is ungrammatical.

passage: For centuries, sailors who traded wool and salt in the northern islands refused to cross the narrow strait between the islands of Harrow and ______ its currents reverse direction four times a day, often with no warning at all.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The first complete sentence says sailors refused to cross the strait, and the second complete sentence explains why. A colon fits before an explanation.
steps: Before the blank: 'For centuries, sailors ... refused to cross the narrow strait between the islands of Harrow and Lune.' Complete sentence.
After the blank: 'its currents reverse direction four times a day...' Complete sentence.
The second sentence gives the reason for the first.
A colon joins two complete sentences when the second explains the first: 'Lune:'.
strategy_tip: Don't let a long first clause fool you; if both sides could end with a period and the second explains the first, use a colon.

rationales.A: Semicolon before a fragment: 'because its currents reverse direction...' can't stand alone, so a semicolon can't come before it.
rationales.B: Comma splice: A comma alone can't join two complete sentences.
rationales.C: Correct. The colon joins two complete sentences, and the second explains why sailors refused to cross.
rationales.D: Run-on sentence: Two complete sentences run together with no punctuation, so 'Lune its currents' reads as one phrase.

passage: When Nadia Ferreol became director of the Ostrand Museum, visitors expected her to rebuild the whole collection. Instead, she made only one change to the main ______ she moved the museum's oldest painting from the entrance to the final room.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The first complete sentence mentions 'only one change', and the second complete sentence says what the change was. A colon introduces that explanation.
steps: Before the blank: 'Instead, she made only one change to the main hall.' Complete sentence.
After the blank: 'she moved the museum's oldest painting from the entrance to the final room.' Complete sentence.
The second sentence names the 'one change'.
Use a colon: 'hall:'.
strategy_tip: When the first clause promises something ('one change') and the second delivers it, a colon goes between them.

rationales.A: Correct. The colon joins two complete sentences, and the second names the one change that the first mentions.
rationales.B: Comma splice: A comma alone can't join two complete sentences.
rationales.C: Broken relative clause: 'which' must stand for a noun inside its own clause, but the words after it already form a complete sentence, so the result is ungrammatical.
rationales.D: Run-on sentence: Two complete sentences run together with no punctuation between them.

topic: a glaze that did not crack
passage: Chemist Lio Arendt mixed a new glaze for ceramic tiles using ash from burned seaweed. He expected the glaze to crack in the kiln at very high ______ the tiles came out smooth and unbroken after every one of his twelve tests.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: 'He expected the glaze to crack...' and 'the tiles came out smooth...' are two complete sentences. A period must separate them, and 'Instead,' begins the second one.
steps: Before the blank: 'He expected the glaze to crack in the kiln at very high temperatures.' Complete sentence.
After the blank: 'the tiles came out smooth and unbroken...' Complete sentence.
'Instead' tells us the second sentence is the opposite of what he expected, so it belongs to the second sentence.
Put a period before 'Instead' and a comma after it.
strategy_tip: Words like 'instead' and 'however' are not joining words; you still need a period or semicolon between the two sentences.

rationales.A: Comma splice: 'instead' is not a joining word like 'and' or 'but', so commas around it can't join two complete sentences.
rationales.B: Correct. The period ends the first sentence, and 'Instead,' opens the second sentence.
rationales.C: Run-on sentence: Two complete sentences run together with no punctuation between them.
rationales.D: Comma splice: The comma after 'instead' joins two complete sentences, and 'instead' wrongly attaches to the first sentence.

topic: a mill left in ruins after a flood
passage: After the flood of 1952, most of the homes in the village of Brede were rebuilt within two years. The old grain ______ was left in ruins for another forty years, until a local history society bought it and restored its water wheel.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: 'The old grain mill was left in ruins...' is one sentence, and 'however' interrupts it between the subject and the verb. An interrupting word needs a comma on both sides.
steps: Read the second sentence without 'however': 'The old grain mill was left in ruins...' It is one sentence.
So 'however' is not joining two sentences; it interrupts one sentence.
An interrupting word takes a comma before it and a comma after it.
Choose 'mill, however,'.
strategy_tip: Before you put a semicolon or period before 'however', check that both sides are complete sentences; if not, use a comma on each side.

rationales.A: Unclosed supplement: 'however' interrupts the sentence, so it needs a comma after it as well as before it.
rationales.B: Semicolon before a fragment: 'The old grain mill' has no verb, so it can't stand before a semicolon.
rationales.C: Correct. The two commas set off 'however', which interrupts the sentence between 'The old grain mill' and 'was left'.
rationales.D: Period after a fragment: 'The old grain mill.' has no verb, so it can't be a sentence.

topic: bakery sales after a station opened
passage: Economist Harriet Vosk studied how a new train station changed business in the town of Mellin. In her 2022 report, Vosk ______ small bakeries near the station had doubled their sales within a year of its opening.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The object of 'found' is the clause 'that small bakeries near the station had doubled their sales'. No punctuation goes between a verb and its object or inside the 'that' clause.
steps: Find the verb: 'found'.
Ask what she found: 'that small bakeries near the station had doubled their sales...' That clause is the object.
A verb and its object are not separated by punctuation, and 'that' is not followed by a comma here.
Choose 'found that' with no punctuation.
strategy_tip: After verbs like 'found', 'showed', or 'argued', a 'that' clause follows directly with no comma or colon.

rationales.A: Splits verb and object: A colon can't come between the verb 'found' and its object, and 'Vosk found' leads straight into what she found.
rationales.B: Splits verb and object: A comma can't come between the verb 'found' and the 'that' clause that is its object.
rationales.C: Splits the that-clause: A comma after 'that' cuts the word off from the subject 'small bakeries' of its own clause.
rationales.D: Correct. The verb 'found' leads directly into its object, 'that small bakeries ... had doubled their sales', with no punctuation.
